title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
raw_text: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs. What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning. As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind. Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. title: Strengthening Europe through public libraries: OMC report to be launched in Dublin
raw_text: Public libraries are part of everyday life. They help people read and learn, access culture, develop digital skills and connect with others. The OMC report brings together evidence of this work and makes the case for stronger support. On Wednesday, 28 October 2026 , the report will be officially launched at an event in Dublin. Strengthening Europe Through Public Libraries was developed by an Open Method of Coordination group (OMC) of 36 experts from 25 EU Member States , with input from neighbouring countries. The group reviewed legislation, national and regional strategies, funding arrangements and more than 100 examples of good practice from across Europe. The scale of the public library network is remarkable. Around 67,000 public libraries across Europe receive an estimated 757 million visits each year and serve 75 million registered users . This gives libraries a unique ability to connect European and national priorities with the needs of local communities. The report looks at ten areas in which public libraries already make an important contribution. These range from literacy, lifelong learning and access to culture to digital inclusion, democratic participation, health and wellbeing, environmental sustainability and community resilience. It describes the modern public library as a marketplace, laboratory, sanctuary and hub: a place for services, learning, new ideas, safety and human connection. title: Call for Expressions of Interest: President’s Panel on International Librarianship Futures
raw_text: As IFLA approaches its centenary, work on the future of libraries and on IFLA100 is well underway. But there is a gap: we lack a shared understanding of international librarianship itself. To address this, IFLA President Leslie Weir has initiated a small, high-level President’s Panel on International Librarianship Futures. Governing Board member Lisa Janicke Hinchliffe has agreed to serve as chair. Today, IFLA is inviting nominations and expressions of interest to help populate the Panel. Why librarianship, and why now? Much of the current futures conversation focuses on libraries: their services, spaces, collections and roles in communities. This Panel adds a complementary focus on librarianship: professional identity, values, education, practice and international connections. The two strands reinforce each other, because libraries can only be as strong as the profession that sustains them. What will the Panel do? Develop a working definition of international librarianship, giving discussions a shared starting point. Identify key considerations for IFLA (members, volunteers, staff and others) in reflecting on the present and future of the profession. Develop a white paper presenting these as a resource, not a policy document, for discussion and adaptation by members and units. The Panel will build on IFLA’s own futures work, including the Trend Report, the Weak Signals Report, Sohail Inayatullah’s WLIC keynote and workshop, and the IFLA100 Futures Quests. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. title: New Version Available: Principles of Transparency and Best Practice in Scholarly Publishing
raw_text: From a Joint Announcement: The Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), the Open Access Scholarly Publishing Association (OASPA), and the World Association of Medical Editors (WAME) are scholarly organisations that have worked together to identify principles of transparency and best practice for scholarly journals. This is the fifth version of a work in progress (published xxxx 2026). We encourage its wide sharing. The Principles of Transparency and Best Practice in Scholarly Publishing apply to all published journal content, including special issues and conference proceedings. Where practices vary from the standards outlined, editors must clearly state the procedures that the journal follows. COPE, DOAJ, OASPA, and WAME agree that these principles are the foundation of good publishing practice and that publishers must demonstrate that they are being met. Because these principles form the basis of eac organisation’s membership criteria, journals and publishers may need to explain when they do not comply with them. title: Enterprises keep buying software upgrades that IT thinks will make things worse
raw_text: Enterprise-sized businesses spend, on average, 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes. Often, those firms' IT heads think those changes are detrimental. Those results are according to a survey of 2,018 chief information officers and senior IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees that Origina commissioned for its report, “ The Software Tax .” About half of the respondents (1,011) are from the US, and the rest are from the United Kingdom. All respondents worked at companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue. Keep in mind that Origina provides maintenance for various enterprise software. Its report points to independent software maintenance as a way for IT leaders to regain control over software budgets, illustrating its potential bias. title: Tesla profits drop 43% in Q3
raw_text: Tesla published its third-quarter 2026 financial results this afternoon. Earlier in October, it reported its sales and deliveries for the three-month period, selling fewer cars than in the same quarter in 2025 , yet it still beat analyst projections. Now we can see how those sales translate to the bottom line. Tesla brought in $28 billion in revenue in Q3, almost the same as in 2025. Automotive revenues were $20.6 billion, a 3 percent decrease year over year. Perhaps more troubling is the decline in revenue from solar panels and storage batteries—this line of business had been growing, but for Q3 revenue fell 16 percent year over year to $2.9 billion. Services and other revenues, though, which include parts and Supercharger use, grew by a third to $4.6 billion. But the company—like the rest of us—has seen its expenses go up. Operating expenses rose by 39 percent to $4.8 billion, dropping the company’s operating margin to just 2.6 percent; in Q3 2025, Tesla’s margin was 5.8 percent. Net profit fell to $787 million, down 43 percent year over year. What’s more, capital expenditures were up by 110 percent to $4.7 billion, and free cash flow was down 62 percent to $1.5 billion. Judge rejects Trump’s wild claim EPA can dismiss data center pollution lawsuits
raw_text: Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI is stuck facing a lawsuit over alleged data center pollution after Donald Trump failed to convince a judge that his Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has complete control over all Clean Air Act lawsuits and can dismiss any suit at whim. Soon after unpermitted gas turbines were discovered powering Musk’s giant Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee, the NAACP sued . Its lawsuit sought an injunction requiring xAI (which, following a merger , is known now as SpaceXAI) to use the best available pollution control technology when operating the turbines and ordering penalties up to $124,426 per day per violation. Without such remedies, the turbines risked drastically spiking pollution in already vulnerable neighborhoods housing predominantly Black communities nearby, the NAACP argued. To block the lawsuit, Trump tried to intervene, arguing that the EPA had the power to unilaterally dismiss lawsuits any time the president decides against enforcing the Clean Air Act. According to Trump, it would supposedly “not serve the public interest” if citizens were allowed to seek massive civil penalties to punish polluting AI firms that were trying to get data centers operational as fast as possible to support Trump’s AI Action Plan . title: Does opting out of smart TV tracking work? Research finds “suspicious” traffic.
raw_text: Smart TVs running operating systems from Samsung, Vizio, and Roku continue sending data to automatic content recognition (ACR) endpoints after users opt out of tracking in the devices’ settings, according to research published on Monday. The paper from Northeastern University researchers points to potential privacy violations from some of the biggest TV brands. ACR captures video screenshots or audio clips from smart TVs and sends the data to remote servers, where it's used for things like measuring content viewership and serving targeted ads. The paper, "Watching the Watchers: Privacy Analysis of US Smart TV Automatic Content Recognition," examined eight smart TV OSes across 12 smart TVs from 10 manufacturers (Amazon, Hisense, LG, Roku, Samsung, Sony, Supersonic, TCL, Vizio, and Westinghouse) to examine when smart TVs use ACR and how effective opting out of user tracking is. title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
raw_text: Hey all, Kartik from Omnara ( https://omnara.com ) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API. You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines. Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada.
